module.title: Python -> Rust Bridge
module.subtitle: Translating Python classes, None, and exceptions into Rust structs, Option, and Result
lesson_points: Rust compiles ahead of time to fast native machine code—it has no garbage collector, so it tracks who owns each value.
Variables in Rust are immutable by default ('let x = 5'); you must opt into changes with 'let mut x = 5'.
Instead of Python's 'None' or raising exceptions, Rust returns 'Option<T>' (Some/None) and 'Result<T, E>' (Ok/Err).

rosetta_pairs.note: In Rust, forgetting 'mut' refuses to compile if you try to reassign or mutate 'fuel'.
Rust separates data fields ('struct') from methods ('impl Ship { ... }').
Rust forces the caller to match Some(val) vs None—null-pointer crashes cannot slip through.

quizzes.title: Option-Style Safe Return
quizzes.prompt: Following Rust's explicit None/Some pattern, what prints when denom = 0?
quizzes.explanation: safe_div(10, 0) returns None cleanly instead of crashing, so the ternary prints 'Empty'.

quizzes.title: Spot the Unhandled None
quizzes.prompt: Click the line that crashes because the caller assumed safe_div() always returns a number (what Rust's Option<T> blocks at compile time!).
quizzes.code:
def safe_div(a, b):
    return None if b == 0 else a / b

val = safe_div(10, 0)
print(val + 1)
quizzes.explanation: Line 5 tries to add 1 to None (TypeError), whereas Rust's Option<f64> forces handling None first.

quizzes.title: Why Make Variables Immutable by Default?
quizzes.prompt: Why does Rust require 'let mut' whenever you want a variable to change later?
quizzes.code: let fuel = 50; // cannot mutate unless 'let mut'
quizzes.sample_explanation: Requiring 'mut' makes every mutation explicit so readers immediately see which values can change and prevents accidental state bugs.
quizzes.explanation: Explicit mutability reduces hidden side effects when reading or refactoring larger programs.
